lessons.title: Know your purpose and your reader
lessons.html:
Workplace writing is writing that helps someone do a job: a notice, a timesheet note, a short report, or instructions. The Government of Canada’s Skills for Success model says writing is the ability to share information using written words, symbols, and images. Official writing steps start with two questions:

  • What is the purpose? (for example, to inform, to explain, to request information, or to give directions)
  • Who is the audience (the reader)?

Then you plan: decide what information to include, how much detail you need, gather facts, and make a simple outline.

The Canada.ca Content Style Guide — official writing rules for Government of Canada web pages — adds habits that also help at work:

  • Most people scan. They do not read every word.
  • Put the most important information first.
  • Speak directly to the reader with you and your.
  • Be direct. Leave out extra background that does not help the reader finish the task.

A later lesson looks at lists and headings. For now, before you write, finish this sentence: “This note is for [who], and I want them to [do or know what].”

This lesson is not about listening and speaking practice (that is the English-practice course) and not about choosing Reply or Reply All (that is the Outlook course). It is about the words on the page.

lessons.title: Canadian spelling and word forms
lessons.html:
The Canada.ca Content Style Guide says Government of Canada content must reflect Canadian writing conventions in English and French. It also says its techniques work together with Writing Tips Plus, a searchable Government of Canada tool for English grammar, punctuation, and writing conventions. If you are not sure how to spell a workplace word in Canadian English, look it up there rather than copying a spelling from another country.

This course teaches only word forms we could open on official pages this session (November 2026). The Canada.ca Content Style Guide says:

  • its shows possession (belonging to it). it’s means it is. Do not mix them up.
  • they’re means they are. their shows possession.
  • Write email (not e-mail), website (not web site), web page (not webpage), and online (not on line).
  • Do not write a whole word in ALL CAPITAL LETTERS.

Common Canadian spellings (from Writing Tips Plus, a Government of Canada tool, checked November 2026):

  • cheque is the Canadian spelling for the bank order. Check is the U.S. spelling.
  • practice (with a c) is the noun: "hockey practice." practise (with an s) is the verb: "I practise every day."
  • colour: Canadians generally prefer the -our ending in words like colour, not -or (color).
  • centre, fibre, theatre: Canadian spelling uses -re for these nouns. Center, fiber, theater are American.
  • metre is the unit of length. A meter is a measuring device.

A computer spell checker may suggest a U.S. spelling. If your workplace follows Canadian English, check the official tool.

lessons.title: Write in plain language
lessons.html:
Plain language means writing so the reader can find what they need, understand it, and use it. The Canada.ca Content Style Guide says this is required for Government of Canada communications, and the same habits make workplace notes easier to read.

Use familiar words. The guide gives examples such as:

  • ask instead of make a request
  • before instead of prior to
  • get instead of obtain
  • to instead of in order to

If you must use a technical word, explain it in short, clear words.

Use the active voice when you can. Name who does the action:

  • Write: “Please send the form to the office by Friday.”
  • Instead of: “The form should be sent by Friday.”

The guide’s own examples include “We may ask you to provide proof of citizenship” (active) rather than “You may be asked…” (passive).

Keep sentences and paragraphs short.

  • Aim for sentences under 15 to 20 words.
  • One main idea in each sentence.
  • One main idea in each paragraph, and no more than three sentences.
  • Start with the subject and the verb so the reader sees who is doing what.

Use lists when you have two or more steps or items. Numbered lists are for order or steps. Bullet lists are for items that are not a ranked sequence.

Read a draft out loud. If you run out of breath, the sentence is probably too long.

lessons.title: Grammar checks and proofreading
lessons.html:
Skills for Success says written words should use correct spelling, punctuation that makes the meaning clear, and correct grammar, including an appropriate verb tense and subject-verb agreement (the verb form should match the subject). It also says to review and revise: proofread for grammar and spelling, then check accuracy, meaning, and tone.

A practical order:

  1. Did you say what you meant? Are names, dates, and numbers correct?
  2. Does each sentence have a clear subject and verb that match? (Write “The boxes are ready,” not “The boxes is ready.”)
  3. Did you use the right time word? If the action already happened, use a past form (“I sent the form yesterday”).
  4. Check its / it’s and their / they’re (Lesson 2).
  5. Check the tone. The Canada.ca Content Style Guide describes a useful workplace tone as direct, informative, conversational, and professional — as if you were speaking to the person, with care.

The style guide also says to read the text out loud, or use a screen reader, to hear what is unclear.

This is not a full grammar textbook. If a sentence still feels wrong, ask a coworker or council tutor to read it. Do not invent rules you have not checked.

Save a copy before you send or post anything important.

lessons.title: Shape a short workplace document
lessons.html:
Skills for Success says to choose a format that fits the task: paragraphs, bullet points, numbered lists, or sub-headings. Official workplace examples include accident report forms, timesheets, and memo boards. Use the form your workplace already has when there is one.

The Canada.ca Content Style Guide says headings should tell the reader what comes next, stay short, and make sense on their own. Use lists so people can scan. Keep list items in the same grammatical pattern (for example, start each step with an action word).

A simple notice or memo (practice layout, not an official government template):

  1. A short title that says what the note is about.
  2. Who it is for, and the date.
  3. The most important point in the first sentence.
  4. Details or steps in a list.
  5. What you want the reader to do, and by when.
  6. Your name.

Example idea: “Water shut-off on Tuesday. The pump room will be closed from 9 am to noon. Please fill bottles on Monday. Thank you, [Name].”

If you will send the note by email, use the Outlook course for To, Cc, subject lines, and Reply All. This lesson is about the words and the shape of the document.

Keep private facts off a shared memo board. Do not post a SIN, a password, or health details other people do not need.

Ask your adult learning council if you want someone to review a practice notice with you.
